idiom_name: compute the payload before super(); class fields initialise after super() returns
implementation_notes: TypeScript spells out the JavaScript order it compiles to - base class fields, base constructor, derived class fields, derived constructor - and requires super() to be called before any this access, while also warning that with target >= ES2022 (or useDefineForClassFields) class fields are initialized after the parent constructor completes and overwrite values the parent set. The classic helper base does not exist in this model (single inheritance, and fields rather than a base-specifier list are the ordering mechanism), so the payload is computed before the super call - into a local, or from a constructor parameter - handed to the parent constructor, and then assigned to the field, which is also what strictPropertyInitialization requires (a readonly field must be definitely assigned in the constructor).
pitfalls: A class field cannot carry the payload to the base: field initializers run after the parent constructor, so the parent sees its own value - the handbook's documented example prints "base", not "derived".

With useDefineForClassFields true (or target ES2022 and later) a field declaration is emitted as a definition that runs after super() and silently overwrites anything the parent constructor assigned; a type-only re-declaration therefore needs declare, not a plain field.

Private fields are inaccessible while the parent constructor runs (TypeError), so a base that calls back into an overridden method cannot read the derived payload - keep such callbacks out of base constructors.
